paper_design_summary: This preregistered online experiment analyzed 400 US Prolific participants after exclusions from 405 recruits; participants were randomly assigned to Control, AI-Single, or AI-Multiple and interpreted three poems with their assigned assistance (pp. 4-6). Pre-generated GPT-4o interpretations remained available during the task in the AI arms, and expert graders scored feature-identification accuracy, interpretive depth and insight, and writing clarity and coherence. These are close-reading proficiency outcomes; the paper reports no eligible creativity or diversity across people's outputs outcome.

studies.label: Close reading of three poems with no, one, or three AI interpretations

assignment.what_was_assigned: Each individual was assigned to Control (no AI interpretation), AI-Single (one pre-generated GPT-4o interpretation), or AI-Multiple (three interpretations), with that condition retained for all poems; poem presentation order was also randomized.
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions (Control, AI-Single and AI-Multiple; Figure 1), applied consistently across all poems.
assignment.locator: p. 4, Sections 3.1.1-3.1.2; individual assignment, between-subjects conditions, and randomized poem order
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 2, footnote 1; p. 6, Section 3.4.2 and footnote 3: https://aspredicted.org/555c-y7kz.pdf. Preregistration is reported in the paper; its separate document was not inspected.

arms.name: Control
arms.description: Close reading each poem without AI assistance

arms.name: AI-Single
arms.description: One pre-generated GPT-4o interpretation displayed under the poem, visible by default

arms.name: AI-Multiple
arms.description: Three pre-generated GPT-4o interpretations in a stacked interface; one visible by default, two more behind labeled buttons

participants.exclusions: 405 recruited; 400 analyzed after excluding participants who completed any poem in excessively short time (3 SDs below the mean). Total and per-arm numbers at randomization are not reported. The arm-size test is printed as chi-squared(2) = 3.815, p = 0.149 (p. 6, Section 3.3).
participants.who: US-based Prolific crowdworkers with 100% approval, English as their primary language, and fluency in English. The paper classifies 51.6% as experienced readers after at least one college-level humanities course and 48.4% as inexperienced (p. 6, Section 3.3).
participants.quote: Our randomized experiment yielded 400 participants in all: 141 in the Control, 115 in the AI-Single, and 144 in the AI-Multiple.
participants.locator: p. 6, Section 3.3: recruitment, exclusions, analyzed total and per-arm counts

ai_tool.how_used: Researchers generated interpretations using the same interpretation-task instructions as participants. AI-Single displayed one interpretation under the poem by default; AI-Multiple provided three distinct interpretations identifying different stylistic features, one visible and two accessible through buttons. This was pre-generated content, with no live chatbot (pp. 4-5, Sections 3.1.2 and 3.1.5; p. 15, Section 6.3.1). Reported AI non-use percentages conflict within the paper and are not treated as settled uptake rates; see notes and reconciliation.

task.description: For each of three poems (Linda Pastan's Love Poem, Marilyn Nelson's Dusting, and Langston Hughes's Theme for English B), participants identified a distinctive word or phrase, a line revealing voice or perspective, and an element of poetic style, explaining each feature's effect in 2-3 sentences. Tasks were adapted from the Critical Reader's Interpretive Toolkit (p. 4, Section 3.1.3). The scored task is analytical interpretation of existing poems, rather than production of creative work or ideas assessed for novelty, originality, usefulness, or overall creativity (pp. 5-6, Section 3.2.1).
task.duration: Around one hour for the whole study (p. 6, Section 3.3)

outcomes.name: Interpretation Quality
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Two expert graders evaluated depth and insight of explanations on a 1-5 rubric (1 = poor, 3 = average, 5 = excellent); scores were averaged across the three tasks within each poem (pp. 5-6, Section 3.2.1). Both graders had English undergraduate degrees and one was an English PhD student; ICC(2,1) = 0.76 is reported for Interpretation Quality and Writing Quality on a validation set of 70 participants (p. 6, Section 3.4.1). The main model uses participant-poem output scores with participant random effects (p. 6, Section 3.4.2). This measures interpretive proficiency, not a reported creativity construct.

outcomes.name: Feature Identification
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Two expert graders scored whether the identified stylistic feature was correct (0 = incorrect/missing; 1 = correct), averaged across the three tasks within each poem (pp. 5-6, Section 3.2.1). Grader agreement was 85.4% on the validation set of 70 participants (p. 6, Section 3.4.1). The main model uses participant-poem output scores with participant random effects (p. 6, Section 3.4.2). This is feature-identification accuracy, not a convergent creativity test.

eligibility.reason: Final review confirms individual random assignment to Control, AI-Single, or AI-Multiple (p. 4, Sections 3.1.1-3.1.2), but criterion 1 includes the creative/ideation-task requirement in codebook Sections 1 and 3. The task asks readers to identify stylistic features and explain their effects in existing poems, assessed as close-reading proficiency (p. 4, Section 3.1.3; pp. 5-6, Section 3.2.1; p. 15, Section 6.3.6), so the full criterion 1 is not met. Criterion 2 is met: 400 people were analyzed after exclusions (Control 141, AI-Single 115, AI-Multiple 144; p. 6, Section 3.3). Criterion 3 is not met: expert graders scored feature correctness, interpretation depth and insight, and writing clarity and coherence, without a reported creativity or across-person diversity outcome (pp. 5-6, Section 3.2.1). Textual overlap compares participants' answers with supplied AI interpretations (p. 11, Section 5.4.1); pleasure measures are self-reports (p. 6, Section 3.2.2). No test after AI removal was conducted (p. 15, Section 6.3.6). The outstanding documentation items do not affect these decisions.

one_line_finding: Among 400 analyzed readers, one GPT-4o interpretation raised interpretation quality by 0.865 points (95% CI [0.664, 1.065]) and writing quality by 1.035 on 1-5 scales, and three interpretations raised them by 0.593 and 0.784 versus Control (pp. 6-7, Table 1), but no eligible creativity or across-person diversity outcome was reported.
open_questions: The source contradicts itself about self-reported AI non-use: the introduction gives 54.8% for AI-Single and 47.0% for AI-Multiple (p. 2), whereas Sections 5 and 5.3 give 45.2% and 53.0% (pp. 9-10). An author correction or original response coding is needed to determine the definitive rates.
Total and per-arm participant counts at randomization, before exclusions, are not stated (p. 6, Section 3.3).
The cited Supplementary Materials, including detailed rubric B.4, are absent from the saved PDF; their contents beyond the main text's descriptions cannot be checked.
notes: Both raw forms parsed. The complete markdown conversion, including references and Appendix A, was read, and recorded statistics were checked against extracted PDF text/tables. The three output-scored proficiency outcomes are retained for audit with question=none; there are no eligible with_ai, across_people, or after_ai outcomes. Criterion 1 applies the codebook's full creative/ideation-task requirement, not merely whether randomization happened. Neither form's criterion-1 value is retained, although both correctly report random assignment. The exclusion does not rest on the absence of novelty alone: the reported tasks and scoring are analytical reading proficiency, and no creative-idea usefulness/appropriateness or overall-creativity measure is reported. Both forms' n_units=1200 was an arithmetic total, not a printed total; n_units is therefore null under the instruction to record only reported numbers. The printed participant-poem instance counts are Control 423, AI-Single 345, AI-Multiple 432 (p. 6, Section 3.3). Total and per-arm randomized counts remain null; recruitment is not treated as assignment. The exclusions description uses the printed recruitment and analyzed counts without deriving an exclusion count. The main models include condition, expertise, poem type and poem position as fixed effects and participant as a random effect (p. 6, Section 3.4.2). The paper calls these pre-registered main analyses (p. 6, Sections 3.4.2 and 4), which is the basis for preregistered_primary; the linked preregistration itself was not inspected. Table 1 gives coefficients with confidence intervals, not printed standard errors (p. 7); regression_coefficient_se is removed from all contrasts. Table 7 gives participant-level mean/SD and Cohen's d, with Holm-Bonferroni adjusted p-values (p. 18). Its p-values printed as 0.000 are preserved as printed, without interpreting them as exact zero. Subgroup sample sizes are absent; the AI-Multiple overall SD is also absent. No effect size or standard error was computed. Self-reported Appreciation, Enjoyment and Self-efficacy are excluded from output outcomes: Table 2 prints ordinal log-odds AI-Single 0.899***, 0.969***, 0.900**, respectively, and AI-Multiple -0.070, -0.248, -0.352, without significance markers (p. 9); Table 8 gives subgroup results (p. 18). Viewing behavior, cursor allocation, self-reported AI use, and AI-answer copying are descriptive engagement measures (pp. 9-13, Section 5). AI-Multiple viewing percentages are 42.1% one interpretation, 12.3% two, and 45.6% three, explicitly percentages of instances rather than unique people (p. 11, Table 3; p. 9, Section 5.1). Lexical overlap and copy rate are computed on answer text, but compare answers with AI interpretations rather than different people's outputs (p. 11, Section 5.4.1; p. 13, Table 6), so they do not qualify as across_people. Self-reported AI non-use remains unresolved: p. 2 gives 54.8% and 47.0%, consistent with Table 4's non-use rows (p. 12), but pp. 9-10 call 45.2% and 53.0% non-use. These rates do not change AI availability: supplied text was available during answer production. The AI benchmark is reported as Feature 1.00, Interpretation 4.00, Writing 4.07 (p. 13, Section 6.1.1), descriptive quality checks rather than a separate eligible creativity experiment. Pilots of n=20, 60, 90, and 100 are described only as instruction development (p. 4, Section 3.1.3), with no separately reported outcome experiment. The paper explicitly omitted a test after AI removal (p. 15, Section 6.3.6). Reconciliation counts substantive omissions and incompatible interpretations, combining each contrast's reported numbers and locators in one entry; paraphrases, differently placed facts, and equivalent source passages are not differences. Shared missing randomized counts are recorded as missing information rather than an A/B disagreement. Version metadata establishes the saved arXiv version; it does not establish a final publisher version. Final review: no c682 challenge files were present. The complete markdown, including references and Appendix A, was read; eligibility passages and the retained numerical results were checked against PDF text and tables. The one-line finding now explicitly labels the sample as analyzed. source.supplement already satisfies the current spec: the cited B materials are absent, while Appendix A is included. The study is an original online randomized experiment, so no reanalysis design-class change applies. All three open questions and the one unresolved reconciliation difference are covered by final.open_items; the AI-use discrepancy is the same item in both lists. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged. Final disposition counts refer only to challenge problems; they are zero because no challenges were supplied.

a.reason: People were randomly assigned to generative-AI assistance (400 analyzed), but the task is close reading of poems (literary interpretation), and the output is scored on correctness of feature identification, interpretive depth, and writing quality. No outcome measures creativity, novelty, originality, or diversity across people, so criterion 3 fails; criterion 1 is unclear only because the task is not a creative or ideation task in the codebook's sense. Remaining outcomes are self-reported pleasure (appreciation, enjoyment, self-efficacy) and a descriptive textual-overlap rate with the AI text.

b.reason: Individuals were randomly assigned to generative-AI interpretations (p. 4) and 400 people were analyzed (p. 6), but the task is analytical close reading of poems and the outputs are scored for feature-identification correctness, interpretation quality (depth and insight), and writing quality, not for creativity, novelty, or diversity across people. The remaining outcomes are self-reported (appreciation, enjoyment, self-efficacy). The only similarity measure is overlap between each participant's answer and the AI text, described for AI arms only, not diversity across people. Criterion 1 is met only in the sense of random assignment to AI; the task is arguably not a creative or ideation task under codebook Section 1.

resolved.reason: Individual random assignment to generative-AI exposure is explicit (p. 4, Sections 3.1.1-3.1.2), and 400 people were analyzed (p. 6, Section 3.3). Criterion 1 is coded using the full codebook definition, including its creative/ideation-task requirement: the present task is foundational analytical close reading of existing poems, assessed as interpretive proficiency, rather than generating creative work or ideas assessed for novelty, originality, usefulness, or overall creativity (p. 4, Section 3.1.3; pp. 5-6, Section 3.2.1; p. 15, Section 6.3.6). Thus randomization itself is confirmed, but the full criterion is not met. Graders do score participants' outputs, yet the outcomes are feature correctness, interpretive depth/insight, and expression clarity/coherence, so the required creativity/diversity construct in criterion 3 is absent. Lexical overlap compares each answer with supplied AI text, not different people's outputs (p. 11, Section 5.4.1); subjective pleasure measures are self-reports (p. 6, Section 3.2.2). No after-AI test was conducted (p. 15, Section 6.3.6).

differences.quote: Our study focused on lay readers and the foundational observation step of close reading—identifying stylistic features and explaining their effects within the text—based on the CRIT framework [62].

open_items.item: Self-reported AI non-use percentages conflict between p. 2 and pp. 9-10 (open_questions[0] and the unresolved reconciliation difference on studies[0].ai_tool.how_used/notes). Original per-poem responses with their use/non-use coding would settle the rates. This concerns uptake, not random assignment or availability of the supplied AI text during production (p. 4, Sections 3.1.1-3.1.2), and affects no eligibility criterion.

Total and per-arm counts at randomization before exclusions are not stated (open_questions[1]; p. 6, Section 3.3). Author confirmation of the assignment counts and exclusion allocation would settle this. Criterion 1 randomization is explicit and criterion 2 uses the confirmed 400 analyzed people, so the missing assignment counts affect no eligibility criterion.

The cited Supplementary Materials, including detailed scoring rubric B.4, are absent from the saved PDF (open_questions[2]; pp. 4-5, Sections 3.1.3-3.1.5; p. 9, Section 5.1). The supplement would settle its exact rubric, task, prompt, survey, and exploratory-analysis contents. The main text explicitly defines the analytical task and all performance measures (pp. 4-6, Sections 3.1.3 and 3.2.1; p. 15, Section 6.3.6), which support the criterion 1 and criterion 3 exclusions; this documentation gap does not make either eligibility decision unclear.
